nameStory: The smooth rose earned its name from being nearly thornless compared to other wild roses – a rare trait that makes it stand out in the prickly rose family. While most roses are armed with sharp thorns, this gentle species has just a few small prickles near its base, making it much smoother to handle than its thorny cousins.
description: Smooth rose is a low-growing wild rose that forms spreading colonies in meadows and prairies. This native shrub reaches about 3 feet tall and produces the classic five-petaled pink roses we associate with wild species. Unlike most roses, it's nearly thornless, with just a few small prickles at the base of its stems, making it much friendlier to touch than other wild roses.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Nearly thornless stems with just a few small prickles at the very base – run your hand along a stem and you'll barely feel any sharp points, unlike other wild roses that are heavily armed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic wild rose flowers with five pink petals and bright yellow centers, about 2 inches across, blooming in early summer with a light, sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating patches of roses rather than single bushes, typically staying under 3 feet tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-7 oval leaflets that have toothed edges and feel smooth to the touch, arranged alternately along the stem

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Round red rose hips about the size of a small marble that persist through fall and winter, feeling firm and slightly waxy when fresh

habitat: Look for smooth rose in open meadows, prairies, and grasslands throughout New England, especially in areas with well-drained soil. It thrives in sunny locations and is often found in old fields, along roadsides, and in natural grassland openings. This species prefers full sun and can tolerate drier conditions than some other native roses.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, and you can easily identify the smooth stems by their lack of thorns.
seasonality.summer: Pink five-petaled flowers bloom in early to mid-summer, attracting bees and other pollinators with their sweet fragrance.
seasonality.fall: Bright red rose hips ripen and leaves may turn yellow before dropping, while the smooth stems become more visible.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red rose hips stand out against snow, and the nearly thornless brown stems are distinctive among bare rose canes.

funFact: Smooth rose is nature's attempt at a 'user-friendly' wild rose – it evolved to be nearly thornless, possibly because it spreads mainly through underground runners rather than needing thorns to protect itself from browsing animals like other roses do.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Carolina rose and other prairie roses, but the nearly thornless stems are the giveaway – if you can run your hand along the stem without getting pricked, you've likely found smooth rose. Other wild roses will have thorns all along their stems.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'prairie rose' in some areas, this species does occur naturally in New England's meadows and grasslands, though it's more common in the Midwest. The variable characteristics mentioned in field guides can make identification tricky, so focus on the smooth stems as your primary clue.
compareHints: Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems. The colony-forming growth habit also sets it apart from the more solitary growth of species like Carolina rose.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
